issues.legal_issue: An Executive Magistrate with the required experience may be appointed as the authority empowered to order release of leased premises even if the experience was gained trying cases triable by a Second Class Magistrate.
material_facts: The officer had served as a Tehsildar for more than three years and was empowered by a general government notification to exercise the powers of a First Class Magistrate.
The officer was posted as an Additional City Magistrate and, under a general notification, exercised the powers of the authority deciding applications for release of leased premises.
The officer granted release after finding the applicants’ residential and business requirements bona fide and their comparative hardship greater.
issues.conclusion: The officer had the requisite experience and was competent to act as the authority and pass the release order.
issues.legal_principle: Section 3(e) of the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972 requires an Executive Magistrate to have not less than three years’ experience as such. Under Schedule III of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, a First Class Magistrate could exercise the powers of a Second Class Magistrate. Accordingly, experience trying cases triable by a Second Class Magistrate could count where the officer also had the powers of a First Class Magistrate; experience trying First Class cases was not necessary.

predicates.release_application_under_rent_law: The officer decided an application seeking release of leased premises under rent-control law.
predicates.executive_magistrate_experience_at_least: The officer had at least three years of experience serving as an Executive Magistrate.
predicates.first_class_magisterial_powers_during_ex: The officer held the powers of a First Class Magistrate while gaining the relevant experience, including experience trying cases within the powers of a Second Class Magistrate.

issues.definition: When an officer deciding a rent-law release application has at least three years’ experience as an Executive Magistrate and held First Class Magistrate powers during that experience, the officer is qualified.

issues.legal_issue: A published government notification conferring magisterial powers cannot be narrowed by a contrary administrative instruction, and communication of the notification through the district administration can satisfy the requirement that the conferment be communicated to the officer.
material_facts: The government issued a general notification conferring First Class Magistrate powers on all Tehsildars and published it in the Official Gazette.
The notification and related material were communicated to Tehsildars through the District Magistrate.

A Deputy Secretary’s note stated that the conferment was confined to maintaining law and order, but the note was an administrative instruction rather than a government order made under the relevant statutory powers.
issues.conclusion: The notification conferred the magisterial powers on the officer, the communication requirement was satisfied, and the administrative note did not restrict the powers to maintaining law and order.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 12 and 39(1)–(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 govern the conferment and communication of magisterial powers. The Court treated the gazetted general notification, its communication through the District Magistrate, and the evidence that it had been acted upon as sufficient; an administrative instruction could not whittle down the government notification.

predicates.government_issued_and_published_general_: The government issued a general grant of powers and published it in the official gazette.
predicates.grant_communicated_through_district_auth: The grant was communicated to the relevant officers through the district administration.
predicates.contrary_limitation_only_in_administrati: Any restriction inconsistent with the published grant appeared only in an administrative instruction, not in a government order exercising the relevant statutory power.

issues.definition: A general grant published and communicated through the district administration extends as stated in the grant when a contrary restriction appears only in an administrative instruction.

issues.legal_issue: An officer’s appointment and acts under colour of lawful authority cannot be impeached by a private litigant through a collateral challenge to the officer’s authority, and the officer’s acts remain effective even if the appointment is defective.
material_facts: A general government notification designated the office of Additional City Magistrate for the relevant area as the authority empowered to decide release applications.
The officer decided the application by virtue of being posted to that office, rather than being appointed as a persona designata.
The challenge to the officer’s competence was raised collaterally in litigation between private parties, and the designating notification was not challenged.
The officer held the office under colour of lawful authority and was not a mere usurper.
issues.conclusion: The officer’s release order could not be impeached on the asserted qualification or appointment defect in the collateral proceeding.
issues.legal_principle: The de facto doctrine, as stated in G. Rangarajan v. Andhra Pradesh, [1981] 3 SCR 474, gives efficacy to acts of an officer who holds office under colour of lawful authority even if the appointment is defective. The doctrine also prevents private litigants from challenging an officer’s title to office collaterally in litigation between them.

predicates.private_litigation_collaterally_challeng: Private litigants challenge an official order by disputing the decision-maker’s authority in proceedings that do not directly determine the decision-maker’s title to office.
predicates.official_held_office_under_colour_of_law: The decision-maker held the office under colour of lawful authority and was not a mere usurper.
predicates.designating_notification_unchallenged: The general notification designating the office to exercise the relevant powers was not challenged.

issues.definition: When private litigants collaterally challenge an order made by an official holding office under colour of lawful authority, while leaving the designating notification unchallenged, the challenge is barred and the order remains effective.

issues.legal_issue: Possession need not be restored for breach of an undertaking when the undertaking was limited to an interim period and the circumstances do not establish that possession was recovered in breach of it.
material_facts: The respondents’ undertaking not to disturb the appellants’ possession was given for a limited period.
The appeal was not disposed of during that period, and the respondents recovered possession nearly two months after the stated period ended.
The Court considered that the respondents may have believed the undertaking had expired and found the alleged breach difficult to sustain.
issues.conclusion: The Court did not order restoration of possession because the alleged breach of the undertaking was not established on the circumstances presented.
issues.legal_principle: The Court assessed the undertaking according to its stated limited duration and the circumstances of the later recovery of possession; it found no sufficient basis to sustain the allegation of breach or to order restoration.

predicates.interim_undertaking_was_time_limited: A party undertook to preserve another party’s possession only for a specified interim period.
predicates.possession_recovered_after_understood_ex: The party recovered possession after the period the party understood the undertaking to cover had ended.
predicates.circumstances_do_not_establish_breach: The surrounding circumstances do not sufficiently establish that the party knowingly acted in breach of the undertaking.

issues.definition: When a time-limited interim undertaking is followed by recovery of possession after the period the party understood it to cover, and the circumstances do not establish breach, possession is not restored.
